forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Halton forecasts £10.74m overspend on special needs funding in 2026/27, taking schools deficit to £38.5m
news_drafts.lead:
Halton's spending on support for children with special educational needs is forecast to reach £42.329m in 2026/27, against funding of £31.593m, an in-year shortfall of £10.74m. The figures are in a report to the council's Schools Forum on 14 October. The funding is the "high needs" block (money for children with special educational needs and disabilities) of the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools).

The report puts the overspend down to three things: expansions in the number and specification of resource bases, rising numbers and costs of high-cost specialist placements in or out of the borough, and more assessments for Education and Health Care Plans, which set out a child's support. Added to the £27.806m deficit carried forward from 2025/26, the cumulative deficit is forecast at £38.542m by the end of 2026/27.

A High Needs Stability Grant, due this autumn, is to cover 90% of deficits built up to the end of March 2026. The report says that would bring the figure down to £13.517m, which includes the 10% of the earlier deficit not covered and the full 2026/27 overspend. The deficit is kept off the council's main balance sheet by a statutory override (a temporary government rule), which is due for review in March 2028.

news_drafts.headline: Halton set its 2026/27 budget with £33.9m of government-approved exceptional financial support
news_drafts.lead:
Halton Borough Council set a balanced budget for 2026/27 only with government approval of £33.9m of exceptional financial support (permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, a last resort). The council's own self-assessment against the financial management standards set by the accountancy body CIPFA, put to its Audit and Governance Board on 30 September, says so directly: it "has set a balanced 2026/27 budget but has required approval from Government of £33.9m of Exceptional Financial Support."

The same document sets out the position beyond this year. The council's medium-term financial strategy (its financial plan, here covering five years to 2031/32) shows that "without the use of Exceptional Financial Support the Council will not be able to set a balanced budget over the 5 year term." The support therefore covers each year from 2027/28 to 2031/32 as well, not 2026/27 alone.

Government oversight runs alongside. The Corporate Overview and Improvement Board was set up in May 2026 as a six-month pilot funded by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) for councils needing this support. It includes council leaders and officers, a Local Government Association regional representative and outside specialists in local government finance. At the end of the six months, in November, its independent members must give MHCLG assurance on Halton's financial recovery plan and position. The board has met five times so far.

news_drafts.headline: Halton Council faces £72m five-year budget deficit despite £29.8m savings plan
news_drafts.lead: Halton Council's five-year financial strategy, presented to the Executive Board on 17 September, forecasts a cumulative budget deficit of £72.567m over the period, even after £29.8m in planned savings. The strategy document states this is "clearly unsustainable" and warns that without exceptional financial support (emergency borrowing from government), the chief finance officer must issue a Section 114 notice (a formal warning that freezes new spending), triggering an emergency council meeting within 21 days. The council has used emergency borrowing for three consecutive years: £10m, £14.7m, and £33.873m. By 2031/32, servicing this emergency borrowing alone will cost £27.504m annually—12.7% of total council resources. A CIPFA review found the financial position "extremely fragile" and concluded the council could not stabilise without continued emergency support.

findings.headline: New resource provisions from September forecast to save approximately £730k annually by reducing high-cost independent special school placements
findings.detail: From September 2026, new primary and secondary resource provisions within existing schools and increased capacity in a mainstream special school are expected to allow learners to remain in mainstream provision rather than requiring Non-Maintained Special School placements. Council forecasts this could prevent approximately 10 such placements at current average cost of £73k per place, delivering a saving of up to 50% of NMSS placement cost.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council is taking active steps to mitigate structural pressures; however, £730k potential saving is modest against £10.74m annual overspend, indicating mitigation addresses only a portion of the problem.
findings.figures: £730k expected saving, 10 placements prevented, £73k average cost per NMSS placement
findings.quote: The expected realised saving could be up to 50% of the NMSS placement cost; the current average cost is £73k per place. By negating the requirement for a NMSS placement for approximately 10 places this could result in a £730k saving.

findings.headline: Structural drivers of High Needs overspend identified as expansions in resource bases, rising specialist placement costs, and growing EHCP assessments
findings.detail: The paper attributes the £10.74m in-year overspend to three factors: significant expansions in numbers and specifications of resource bases; increasing numbers and costs of high-cost specialist placements in or out of borough; and increases in numbers and value of EHCP assessments. These are explicitly described as factors that 'will continue to be material ongoing pressures.'
findings.matters: These drivers are largely outside council control and indicate pressure will persist beyond 2026/27 even with mitigation steps; signals ongoing structural deficit risk.
findings.figures: £10.74m in-year overspend, three identified structural drivers
findings.quote: The overspend is in the main due to a) significant expansions in numbers and specifications of resource bases, b) increasing numbers and costs of high-cost specialist placements in or out of Borough, and c) increases in numbers and value of EHCP (Education & Health Care Plan) assessments.

findings.headline: Statutory override mechanism keeping DSG deficit off council balance sheet due for review in March 2028
findings.detail: DSG deficits are currently kept off the council's balance sheet through statutory override, a mechanism that has been extended and is now due for review effective March 2028. If not extended, the £13.517m residual cumulative deficit (after grant) would transfer to the council's balance sheet from that date.
findings.matters: Creates material uncertainty about future balance sheet position and reported borrowing capacity; if override ends, a £13.5m+ deficit could impact council credit rating and borrowing terms.
findings.figures: March 2028 review date, £13.517m cumulative residual deficit
findings.quote: Such deficits in all Local Authorities are currently kept off the council balance sheet by what is known as a statutory override. This mechanism has already been extended and is now due for review effective March 2028.

findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit forecast to reach £38.542m by end 2026/27, reducing to £13.517m after High Needs Stability Grant
findings.detail: Cumulative deficit brought forward from 2025/26 (£27.806m) plus in-year overspend (£10.736m) totals £38.542m. A High Needs Stability Grant, to be received in Autumn 2026, will cover 90% of accumulated deficits accumulated up to end-March 2026, reducing the figure to £13.517m—though this leaves £2.781m (10% residual) plus the full 2026/27 overspend unresolved.
findings.matters: Government support covers historical deficit but not ongoing structural overspend; demonstrates material reliance on one-off grant support rather than structural resolution of the underlying cost pressure.
findings.figures: £27.806m brought forward, £10.736m in-year, £38.542m cumulative, £13.517m after grant, 90% grant coverage of pre-2026/27 deficit
findings.quote: the cumulative forecast deficit by the end of 2026/27 is £38.542m. 90% of Authorities' DSG High Needs accumulated up to end-March 2026 are due to be covered this Autumn with the receipt of High Needs Stability Grant.

findings.headline: High Needs Block forecast expenditure of £42.329m exceeds allocation of £31.593m by £10.74m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The High Needs Block has gross allocation of £31.593m. After FE recoupment of £5.123m, net allocation is £26.469m. Projected full-year expenditure is £42.329m, creating an in-year shortfall of £10.735m. The overspend is driven by significant expansions in resource bases, increasing numbers and costs of high-cost specialist placements in or out of borough, and increases in EHCP assessments.
findings.matters: High Needs spending is a structural pressure on councils, and this shows demand significantly exceeds government funding allocation, indicating unmet need that must be managed within the council's own resources.
findings.quote: Projected full year expenditure for all anticipated demands on High Needs funding is £42.329m, which is a substantial amount (£10.74m) in excess of the present High Needs allocation of £31.593m.
